static-083.q: What is the magnitude of the charge of one electron, in coulombs? (Type like 1.6e-19)

hist-040.q: Which unit is used to measure electric charge?

hist-041.q: Which unit measures electric current, the flow of charge per second?

new.q: In 1820 Ørsted saw a compass needle swing when it was placed near a wire carrying current. What did this show?
o: A current produces a magnetic effect
Static charge on the wire pulls on iron
The wire was heating the air around the needle
Gravity from the wire bends the needle
new.w: Ørsted's compass result was the first link between electricity and magnetism.
sol: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, so it only reacts to magnetic effects.
The needle moved only while current flowed, so the current made the magnetic effect.
Heat and static charge do not turn a compass; this was a new discovery.

new.q: Which scientist discovered in 1820 that a current deflects a compass needle? (Spell it any way you like.)
new.w: Hans Christian Ørsted (also spelled Oersted) found the first electricity and magnetism link.
sol: Only a magnetic effect from the wire can turn it.

new.q: What could the voltaic pile of 1800 do that rubbing amber or glass could not?
new.w: Volta's pile was the first source of steady current instead of one-shot static sparks.
sol: A pile uses chemical reactions between metals and a wet cloth, which keep going.
A steady current is what circuits need.

new.q: Who is credited with naming the two kinds of charge positive and negative?
new.w: Benjamin Franklin introduced + and − and the idea of conventional current.
sol: His guess about flow direction is why conventional current runs + to −.

new.q: In Boole's algebra, what is 1 AND 0?
new.w: AND gives 1 only when every input is 1.
sol: AND means both must be true.

new.q: In Boole's algebra, what is 1 OR 0?
new.w: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1.
sol: OR means either one is enough.

new.q: Which unit is named for the Scottish engineer James Watt?
o: The watt, a unit of power
The volt, a unit of potential difference
The joule, a unit of charge
The farad, a unit of energy
new.w: The watt measures power: energy per second.
sol: Watt, volt and farad are all people's names.
The watt is the rate of using energy.
One watt = one joule per second.

new.q: US wall outlets supply alternating current. How many cycles per second (in Hz) does it go through?
new.w: In the US, mains AC is 60 Hz (50 Hz in much of the world).
sol: AC reverses direction again and again.

new.q: Put these in order, earliest first.
sol: Coulomb is the earliest, from the 1780s.
Faraday found induction in 1831, and Hertz made radio waves in 1887.

new.q: Which scientist is matched with the quantity their unit measures?
new.w: The farad is the unit of capacitance.
sol: Hertz = frequency, Ohm = resistance, Volta = voltage.

new.q: The ancient Greek word for amber, which Thales noticed attracts light objects after rubbing, gave us which modern word?
new.w: Greek elektron means amber; rubbed amber showed static electricity.
sol: Amber was one of the first known things to show static charge.
Magnetism comes from lodestones, a different story.

new.q: Match each unit to what it equals.
new.w: Each unit is a ratio of other quantities.
sol: Voltage is energy per charge; resistance is voltage per current.
Power is energy per time; capacitance is charge per volt.

new.q: Ørsted showed that a current makes a magnetic effect. Faraday's discovery is the reverse. What is it?
o: A changing magnetic field can create a voltage and current
A current cannot flow in a magnet
Static charge can make a magnet
new.w: Ørsted: electricity to magnetism. Faraday: magnetism to electricity.
sol: Faraday moved magnets near coils in 1831.
A changing magnetic field pushes charges, giving a voltage (induction).

new.q: A power-plant generator turns a magnet inside coils of wire. Whose discovery does it use?
new.w: Moving magnets near coils induces a voltage: induction.
sol: Generators need a changing magnetic field through a coil.
Volta's pile is a chemical battery and has no motion.

new.q: AC power at 60 Hz goes through how many complete cycles in 3.0 s?
new.w: 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
sol: A common slip is to give 60, one second's worth.

new.q: What is the period of 50 Hz AC, in milliseconds?
new.w: Period = 1 / frequency.

new.q: What is the period of 60 Hz AC, in milliseconds? Round to 0.1.
new.w: Period = 1 / frequency.

new.q: In 1937 Claude Shannon showed that Boole's algebra could describe what?
o: Networks of relay and switch circuits
new.w: Boole's 0 and 1 map onto open and closed switches.
sol: Switch on or off is two-valued, like Boole's 0 and 1.
Shannon used Boolean algebra to design switching circuits.
This is the basis of digital logic.

new.q: Kirchhoff's current law: 5.0 A flows into a junction. 2.0 A leaves in one wire and 1.5 A in another. What current leaves in the third wire?
new.w: Charge in equals charge out at a node.
sol: Charge cannot pile up at a node.

new.q: Why did power companies choose AC for long-distance power lines?
o: Transformers can step the voltage up, which lowers the current and the heat loss in the wires
AC electrons move faster than DC electrons
new.w: High voltage means low current, and low current wastes little power as heat.
sol: Wire loss is I²R, so lower current wastes much less.
Transformers work only with changing (AC) current.
AC wires still have resistance, and DC lights bulbs fine.

new.q: Match each scientist to the unit named for them.
new.w: Many SI electrical units honor these scientists.

new.q: Name the American scientist whose name is on the unit of inductance (the henry).
new.w: Joseph Henry discovered induction independently of Faraday.

new.q: Galvani saw frog legs twitch near two different metals. Volta argued the electricity came from:
o: the contact of the two different metals
new.w: Volta's view led to the pile: two metals plus an electrolyte.
sol: Galvani thought the frog made the electricity.
Volta tested stacks of metal and found current without any animal.
That led to the first battery.

new.q: Franklin guessed that current flows from + to −. We now know that in a metal wire the moving charges are electrons. Why do we still use Franklin's 'conventional current'?
o: Circuit rules give the same results either way, and the convention is standard
Electrons really do flow from + to −
Franklin's rule makes the math work only for batteries
new.w: Conventional current is a bookkeeping choice that still works.
sol: A positive charge moving one way acts like a negative charge moving the other way.
So the rules for V, I and R stay valid.

new.q: Who discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays?
new.w: J. J. Thomson showed cathode rays are tiny negative particles.
sol: Cathode rays bend in electric fields toward +.
Thomson named them electrons (corpuscles at first).

new.q: In the 'war of the currents', Edison's early power stations supplied which type of electricity?
new.w: Edison used DC; Tesla and Westinghouse promoted AC.
sol: Edison's 1880s New York system used DC.
AC won for long lines because transformers could raise voltage.

new.q: The Leyden jar of the 1740s stored charge. Which modern part does it most resemble?
new.w: Two conductors (foil inside and out) separated by glass hold charge: a capacitor.
sol: It stored charge between two conducting layers.
That is what a capacitor does.

new.q: Put these events in order, earliest first.
sol: Ørsted and Faraday are in the first half of the 1800s.

new.q: Which unit equals one joule per second?
new.w: Power is energy per time.
sol: One joule per second is one watt.

new.q: Which scientist's name is on the unit of magnetic flux density?
new.w: The tesla (T) measures magnetic flux density.
sol: The unit of flux density is the tesla.
It is named for Nikola Tesla.

new.q: Select ALL that are SI units named for scientists.
new.w: Second is a time unit with no person's name.
sol: Volta, Hertz and Faraday are all honored.
The second is not named after anyone.
So volt, hertz and farad are the correct picks.

new.q: Before the voltaic pile (1800), experimenters mostly had which sources of electricity?
new.w: Only static sources existed until Volta.
sol: They could make sparks by rubbing.
Leyden jars stored that charge briefly.
No steady source existed until the pile.

new.q: Coulomb's law of electric force and Newton's law of gravity share which feature?
o: Force falls off with the square of the distance
new.w: Both are inverse-square laws, but electric force can repel and is far stronger.
sol: Electric force depends on charge, not mass, and can push or pull.

new.q: A wire with current is held over a compass. How does the needle behave?
o: It turns away from its north-pointing direction
It stays still because current has no magnetic effect
It points straight at the wire
new.w: Current makes a magnetic field that the compass needle follows.
sol: The needle follows the combined field of Earth and the wire.
It does not spin or point at the wire.

new.q: A pile has 30 identical cells in series, each giving 0.90 V. What is the total voltage?
new.w: Series voltages add.

new.q: One ohm is equal to one:
new.w: Ohm's law R = V/I.
sol: Coulomb per second is the ampere; joule per coulomb is the volt.

new.q: One watt is equal to one:
new.w: Power P = V × I.

new.q: A 10 kW load is fed through a line with 2.0 Ω resistance at 1000 V. How many watts are lost as heat in the line?
new.w: Current I = P/V, loss = I²R.
sol: Do not use V²/R: 1000 V is the supply voltage, not the voltage across the line.

new.q: Sending the same power at 10 times higher voltage cuts the line's heat loss by what factor?
new.w: Loss = I²R and I = P/V.
sol: 10 times the voltage means 1/10 the current.

new.q: A plant sends 50 kW through lines with total resistance 0.40 Ω at 500 V. What percent of the power is lost in the lines?
new.w: I = 100 A, so loss = 4000 W.

new.q: The same plant (50 kW, 0.40 Ω line) steps up to 5000 V. How many watts are lost in the lines?
new.w: I falls to 10 A.
sol: = 40 W, 100 times less than at 500 V.

new.q: A transformer is wired to a steady DC battery. After the switch is closed, the output voltage is zero. Why?
o: Induction needs a changing magnetic field, and steady DC gives a constant one
Transformers only work with static charge
The primary coil has no resistance
new.w: Faraday's induction needs changing flux.
sol: A constant current makes a constant magnetic field.
A coil only gets a voltage when the field through it changes.
AC changes all the time, so transformers use AC.

new.q: Which statement best contrasts Ørsted and Faraday?
o: Ørsted: current makes a magnetic effect. Faraday: a changing magnetic field makes a voltage
Ørsted: magnets make current. Faraday: current makes magnets
Both showed that static charge makes magnets
new.w: They are opposite directions of the same link.
sol: Ørsted (1820) went from electricity to magnetism.
Faraday (1831) went from magnetism to electricity.
Mixing the two is the common error.

new.q: A magnet is held perfectly still inside a coil connected to a meter. What current does the meter show?
o: A steady current proportional to the magnet's strength
A current that grows with time
new.w: Induction needs change, not just a magnetic field.
sol: Faraday found a current only while the field changes.
A still magnet means no change in flux.

new.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil first slowly, then quickly. Compared with the slow push, the quick push gives:
new.w: Induced voltage depends on how fast the magnetic flux changes.
sol: Induced voltage grows with the rate of change.
Speed matters, not just the magnet's presence.

new.q: A magnet pushed into a coil over 0.50 s induces 0.40 V. If the same push takes 0.10 s, how many volts are induced?
new.w: Induced voltage ∝ rate of change of flux (1/time).

new.q: A coil gives 0.40 V. Now the magnet moves twice as fast through a coil with twice as many turns. How many volts?
new.w: Voltage ∝ turns × speed.
sol: Twice the speed doubles the voltage.
Twice the turns doubles it again.

new.q: Hertz's radio-wave experiments of the 1880s confirmed whose prediction?
new.w: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves; Hertz made and detected them.
sol: Maxwell's equations predicted waves moving at light speed.
Hertz generated them with sparks and detected them across a room.
He also showed they reflect and refract like light.

new.q: Hertz showed radio waves reflect, bend and polarize like light. What did this suggest about light?
o: Light is also an electromagnetic wave
Light is a flow of electrons in a wire
Light is a magnetic field only
new.w: Same behavior pointed to the same kind of wave.
sol: They act like light in many tests.
So light is an electromagnetic wave of higher frequency.

new.q: A radio station transmits at 100 MHz. What is the wavelength in meters? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
new.w: Wavelength = c / f.

new.q: A transmitter makes waves 0.60 m long. What is their frequency in MHz? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
new.w: f = c / λ.

new.q: Evaluate in Boole's algebra: (1 AND 0) OR (NOT 0). Give 0 or 1.
new.w: Work the brackets first.

new.q: Evaluate NOT(A AND B) OR C for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. Give 0 or 1.
new.w: Work inside out.

new.q: De Morgan (a contemporary of Boole) showed that NOT(A AND B) equals:
new.w: Test with A = 1, B = 0: NOT(0) = 1 and (0 OR 1) = 1.
sol: Try A=1, B=0: A AND B = 0, so NOT gives 1.

new.q: How many different input combinations does a 4-input Boolean circuit have?
new.w: Each input has 2 values.

new.q: The I–V graph of a light-bulb filament curves, because its resistance rises as it heats up. What does that say about Ohm's law V = IR?
o: R = V/I still defines resistance at each point, but R is not constant
Ohm's law is false for all conductors
The bulb has zero resistance when cold
The current is independent of voltage
new.w: Ohm's 'law' means constant R; V/I is still defined everywhere.
sol: A straight I–V line means constant R (ohmic).
A curve means R changes with V (temperature).
V = IR still works as a definition at each point.

new.q: Ohm found that doubling the voltage across a metal wire at steady temperature does what to the current?
new.w: I = V/R with R constant.
sol: Current ∝ voltage for an ohmic wire.

new.q: Coulomb's torsion balance twists 8.0° when two charged spheres are 0.10 m apart. Twist is proportional to force. How many degrees will it twist at 0.05 m, with the same charges?
new.w: Halving r multiplies force by 4.
sol: Half the distance gives 4 times the force.

new.q: Why was a stack of metal discs separated by wet (brine-soaked) cloth able to make current?
o: The brine lets ions move between the two metals so each cell completes its circuit
The cloth insulates so no charge moves
The brine supplies electrons by itself
new.w: Two metals plus an electrolyte make a chemical cell.
sol: A cell needs two unlike metals and an electrolyte.
Ions carry charge through the brine.
Stacking cells in series adds voltage.

new.q: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction and attract. If the current in one wire is reversed, the force becomes:
new.w: Ampère: same-direction currents attract, opposite-direction currents repel.
sol: Reversing one current flips the force.

new.q: A 9.0 V cell and a 3.0 V cell are in series but facing each other (opposing) across a 12 Ω resistor. How much current flows, in amperes?
new.w: Net voltage is the difference.
sol: Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop.

new.q: Kirchhoff's current law: 3.2 A and 1.1 A flow into a junction and 2.0 A flows out one wire. What current flows out of the other wire?
new.w: In = out.

new.q: Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909) found that the charge on each drop was:
o: a whole-number multiple of one smallest charge
new.w: Charge is quantized in units of e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
sol: No fractions of e were seen.
That showed charge comes in lumps.

new.q: Which expression equals one watt?
new.w: P = I²R.
sol: P = VI and V = IR, so P = I²R.

new.q: Which named unit equals one ampere × one ohm?
new.w: V = IR.

new.q: Match each discovery to the year (best-known date).
new.w: A timeline helps tie names to ideas.

new.q: Siemens (S) is the SI unit of conductance, honoring Werner von Siemens. How is it related to the ohm?
new.w: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.

new.q: Millikan, Thomson and Coulomb all helped explain charge. Which is matched correctly?
new.w: Thomson found the electron (1897); Millikan measured its charge (1909).

new.q: Tesla's AC induction motor spins without electrical contact to its rotor. What lets the rotor turn?
o: A rotating magnetic field induces current in the rotor
new.w: Faraday induction plus a rotating field (from polyphase AC).
sol: Polyphase AC makes a rotating magnetic field.
That field induces currents in the rotor.
The induced currents feel a force, so the rotor turns.

new.q: A student says: 'Ohm's law shows current is used up as it passes through resistors.' Which Kirchhoff idea corrects this?
o: Charge is conserved, so the current is the same coming out of a series resistor as going in
Voltage is used up so current is too
new.w: Current is flow of charge, which cannot vanish.
sol: Energy, not current, is used up (the voltage drops).
This is the voltage-law and current-law contrast.

new.q: Which pair correctly links the history to the physical law each person found?
o: Kirchhoff: charge and energy are conserved in circuits
Ohm: charge is conserved at nodes
Volta: energy is conserved around loops
new.w: KCL = charge conservation; KVL = energy conservation.
sol: Hertz did waves; Coulomb did the force law.

new.q: A balloon rubbed on hair gains electrons. The balloon is now:
new.w: Gaining electrons makes an object negative.
sol: More electrons than protons means net negative.

new.q: Which particles move when an object is charged by rubbing?
new.w: Only electrons are free to move between materials.
sol: Electrons are loosely held at the outside.

new.q: Which material holds static charge best?
new.w: Insulators keep charge in place; conductors let it spread and escape.
sol: Charge cannot easily leave an insulator.

new.q: A neutral object contains:
o: equal amounts of positive and negative charge
new.w: Neutral means the charges balance, not that they are absent.

new.q: Electric field arrows around an isolated positive point charge point:
new.w: Field points the way a positive test charge is pushed.
sol: A positive test charge is repelled by +.

new.q: Which of these is a good conductor?
new.w: Metals have free electrons.
sol: Rubber, wood and glass are insulators.

new.q: Electric field lines drawn closer together show where the field is:
new.w: Line density shows field strength.
sol: More lines per area means stronger field.

new.q: Silk rubbed on glass gives the glass +2 nC of charge. What happens to the silk?
new.w: Charge is conserved: the total stays zero.
sol: Electrons moved from glass to silk.

new.q: Proton and electron charges compared: they are
o: equal in size and opposite in sign
equal in size and the same sign
new.w: Both have magnitude 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
sol: That is why atoms are neutral.

new.q: Two charges, +2.0 µC and +3.0 µC, are 0.60 m apart. Find the force between them in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: F = kq₁q₂/r².

new.q: A rod gains 5.0×10¹² extra electrons. What is its charge in µC? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; give the magnitude)
new.w: Q = ne.

new.q: A 5.0 nC test charge feels a force of 2.0×10⁻⁴ N. What is the electric field strength, in N/C?
new.w: E = F/q.

new.q: A 4.0 µC charge sits in a field of 2500 N/C. What force acts on it, in newtons?
new.w: F = qE.
sol: Rearrange E = F/q to F = qE.

new.q: A charged metal sphere (+6 µC) touches an identical neutral sphere, then they are separated. Each sphere has:
new.w: Identical conductors share total charge equally.
sol: Two identical spheres split it evenly.

new.q: A negatively charged rod is brought near, not touching, the knob of a neutral electroscope. The leaves:
o: spread apart, then collapse when the rod is removed
spread and stay spread after the rod leaves
new.w: Charge is only shifted, not added.
sol: The rod pushes electrons down to the leaves.
The leaves repel, so they spread.
Remove the rod and the electrons return, so they collapse.

new.q: A positive rod touches a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand, then is removed. The sphere is:
new.w: Conduction gives the same sign as the rod.
sol: Electrons flow from the sphere to the rod.

new.q: One of two point charges is cut to half its value. The distance stays the same. The force becomes:
new.w: Force ∝ q₁q₂.
sol: Force is proportional to each charge.
Half a charge gives half the force.
Only distance has the squared effect.

new.q: On a conductor in equilibrium, excess charge sits:
new.w: Like charges repel and spread out as far as possible.
sol: They move to the outside surface.
Inside a conductor in equilibrium the field is zero.

new.q: An electron is placed in an electric field that points east. The force on the electron points:
new.w: Force on a negative charge is opposite to the field.
sol: Field direction = force on a positive test charge.
So its force is opposite: west.

new.q: Why can electric field lines never cross?
o: The field has one direction at any point
new.w: At a crossing, the field would have two directions at once.
sol: Each point has a single field direction.

new.q: Why are fuel trucks grounded or bonded to the tank when they fuel?
o: To drain static charge so a spark cannot ignite fuel vapor
To make the fuel flow faster
new.w: Sparks can ignite vapor; grounding drains the charge.
sol: Grounding lets charge leak away safely.

new.q: Which charge could exist on an object? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
new.w: Charge is quantized: a whole number times e.
sol: Fractions of e do not appear.

new.q: A body has a charge of −4.806×10⁻¹⁹ C. How many excess electrons does it have? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
new.w: N = Q/e.

new.q: A charged object comes near a neutral insulator, shifting its charges slightly without a net charge change. What is this called?
new.w: The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes.
sol: Insulator charges cannot flow, only shift.
It explains why balloons stick to walls.

new.q: Why does a charged balloon on a wall fall after a while?
o: Charge leaks away through the air and wall
new.w: Moist air and surfaces slowly drain charge.
sol: Charge is not permanent on an insulator in air.
Less charge means weaker attraction, so gravity wins.

new.q: Why does a pointed lightning rod help protect a building?
o: Charge concentrates at points, bleeding off gently or giving lightning a safe path to ground
It attracts no charge at all
new.w: Sharp points concentrate field and lead charge safely to ground.
sol: A conducting path to ground carries the current away.
This keeps it from going through the building.

new.q: A car is hit by lightning. Why are the passengers usually safe?
o: Charge flows along the metal outside, and the field inside is near zero
Rubber tires insulate the car from the strike
new.w: A conducting shell shields its inside.
sol: Charge spreads on the outer surface.
The field inside a conductor shell is about zero.
Tires alone cannot stop a lightning strike.

new.q: Match each charging process to its description.
pairs: Electrons move between two rubbed materials
Touching shares charge, giving the same sign
Charge separated by a nearby rod and then grounded
Charges in an insulator shift, with no net change
new.w: Four ways to move or rearrange charge.
sol: Induction needs grounding; polarization leaves net charge zero.

new.q: Put the steps of safely handling a static-sensitive chip in order.
items: Put on a wrist strap connected to ground
Take the chip out of its antistatic bag
Place the chip in the socket
new.w: Ground yourself before touching the chip.

new.q: Distance between two charges is halved. The force becomes:
new.w: Force ∝ 1/r².

new.q: Charges 1.5 µC and 2.5 µC are 3.0 cm apart. Find the force in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: Convert cm to m before squaring.
sol: ≈ 37 N; forgetting to convert gives a nonsense number.

new.q: Two charges exert 9.0 N on each other at 0.10 m. At what distance would the force be 1.0 N? Answer in meters.
new.w: Force ∝ 1/r².

new.q: A 40 N force acts at distance r. Charge 1 triples, charge 2 is halved, and the distance doubles. New force in newtons?
new.w: Multiply the factors.

new.q: Distance tripled and both charges doubled. The new force is:
new.w: Charges give 2 × 2 = 4; distance gives 1/9.

new.q: q₁ is halved, q₂ is tripled, and the distance is halved. The force becomes:
new.w: Factor = (½ × 3)/(½)².

new.q: A +4q sphere and a +q sphere repel. Which statement is right?
o: The forces on the two spheres are equal in size and opposite in direction
The +4q sphere feels 4 times more force
The +q sphere feels 4 times more force
Only the smaller sphere feels a force
new.w: Newton's third law: they act on each other with equal forces.
sol: Each charge's field acts on the other.
Bigger charge does not mean bigger force on it.

new.q: Two identical-mass balls on strings repel; one has charge +4q, the other +q. Both hang at rest. Compared with each other, the string angles are:
o: the +4q ball hangs at a larger angle
the +q ball hangs at a larger angle
new.w: Equal forces on equal masses give equal angles.
sol: The Coulomb forces are equal (third law).
Same force balance means same angle.

new.q: A neutral metal ball hangs near a positive rod. It swings in, touches the rod, then:
new.w: After touching, it has the same sign as the rod, so it is repelled.
sol: Now both positive, so it is repelled.

new.q: A negatively charged electroscope has spread leaves. A positive rod is brought near the knob (no contact). The leaves:
new.w: The rod pulls electrons up toward the knob, leaving the leaves less negative.
sol: They move up, so the leaves hold less charge.
Less repulsion, so they close up.

new.q: A positive rod is brought near a neutral metal sphere on an insulator. The sphere is grounded briefly, then the ground is removed, then the rod is removed. The sphere is now:
new.w: Induction leaves the opposite sign.
sol: The rod attracts electrons from ground.

new.q: Two identical positive charges are fixed. Along the line between them, where could a third negative charge feel zero net force?
new.w: Equal pulls cancel only at the midpoint.
sol: Only at the midpoint are distances equal.
So net force is zero only there.

new.q: A +q and a −q are fixed 1 m apart. On the straight line through them, where can a small positive test charge feel zero net force?
new.w: Between them the forces add; outside, the nearer charge always wins.
sol: At the midpoint both forces point the same way, so they add.
Outside, the nearer charge exerts the stronger force.
The charges are equal in size, so they never cancel.

new.q: At the midpoint between +q and −q, the electric field points:
o: toward −q, and is twice one charge's field
new.w: Both fields point the same way there.

new.q: At the midpoint between two equal positive charges, the electric field is:
new.w: The two fields point in opposite directions with equal size.
sol: At the midpoint the pushes are opposite.

new.q: A charged comb picks up a bit of paper. Soon the paper jumps off. Why?
o: It gained the comb's charge by contact, so it is repelled
new.w: Polarization first, then conduction.
sol: Now the same sign, so repulsion.

new.q: Why do paint droplets from an electrostatic sprayer spread out evenly and coat the object's back?
o: Droplets have like charge so they repel; the grounded object attracts them
new.w: Like charges repel; opposite (or induced) attract.
sol: Droplets all carry the same sign.
The object attracts them, even to its back.

new.q: A wrist strap for electronics work has a 1 MΩ resistor in it. Why is that resistor there?
o: To limit current if the wearer touches a live circuit
To build up charge on the wearer
To speed up discharge to zero seconds
To make the strap a perfect insulator
new.w: It still drains static slowly but limits dangerous current.
sol: Static charge is tiny and drains fine through 1 MΩ.
A direct wire would be a shock hazard.
So the resistor keeps it safe.

new.q: Select ALL true statements about a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
o: Excess charge is on the surface
Field lines meet the surface at right angles
Charge spreads perfectly evenly on every shape
new.w: Charge crowds at sharp points, so it is not uniform.
sol: Free charges stop moving when the field inside is zero.
They sit on the surface; the field at the surface is perpendicular.
On pointed shapes charge is denser at the tips.

new.q: Select ALL actions that reduce static buildup.
o: Walking on carpet in rubber-soled shoes
new.w: Rubber-soled shoes on carpet help build charge.
sol: Rubber on carpet insulates and charges you.

new.q: A 3.0 nC point charge. Use E = F/q with Coulomb's law to find the field at 0.30 m from it, in N/C. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: E = kq/r².
sol: Place a test charge q₀ there: F = kqq₀/r².

new.q: A 1.0 mA current flows for 3.2 ms. How many electrons pass a point? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
new.w: Q = It, then N = Q/e.

new.q: Air breaks down and sparks when the field reaches about 3×10⁶ V/m. About how many volts across a 1.0 mm gap before a spark? (field × gap)
new.w: V = E × d.

new.q: A rod loses 3.0×10¹² electrons. What is its charge in µC? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; give the magnitude)
new.w: Q = ne.
sol: Losing electrons leaves the rod positive.

new.q: Two equal charges repel with 0.90 N at 0.10 m. Find each charge, in µC. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: q² = Fr²/k.

new.q: Two +2.0 µC charges repel with 0.20 N. How far apart are they, in meters? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: r² = kq₁q₂/F.

new.q: +8.0 µC and −2.0 µC identical spheres attract. They touch and are returned to 0.30 m apart. What is the new force in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: Total charge splits evenly after touching.
sol: Total = +6.0 µC, so each sphere has +3.0 µC.

new.q: Identical spheres of −10 µC and +6.0 µC touch and are separated. What is the charge on each, in µC?
new.w: Total is conserved and shared.

new.q: Sphere A has charge Q. It touches identical neutral sphere B, is separated, then touches identical neutral sphere C. What fraction of Q does A end with? (decimal)
new.w: Each touch splits A's charge in half.

new.q: An electron (m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) sits in a field of 2.0×10³ N/C. What is its acceleration in m/s²? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
new.w: F = eE, a = F/m.
sol: ≈ 3.5×10¹⁴ m/s²: huge, since electrons are so light.

new.q: A −2.0 µC charge sits between +4.0 µC (0.20 m to its left) and +1.0 µC (0.30 m to its right). Find the net force magnitude in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: Both attract, in opposite directions.
sol: Opposite directions, so subtract: ≈ 1.6 N toward the +4.0 µC.

new.q: A +2.0 µC charge sits midway between +4.0 µC and +1.0 µC charges 0.60 m apart. What is the net force in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: Both repel; the pushes oppose.
sol: Pushes: 0.80 N and 0.20 N in opposite directions.
Net ≈ 0.60 N toward the +1.0 µC charge.

new.q: Charges +4q and +q are 0.90 m apart. How far from the +4q is the point on the line between them where the net field is zero? (meters)
new.w: Equal fields: 4/x² = 1/(d−x)².

new.q: +4.0 µC and −1.0 µC are 0.50 m apart. On the line beyond the −1.0 µC (away from the +4.0 µC), where is the net field zero? Give the distance from the −1.0 µC in meters.
new.w: Equal and opposite fields: 4/(0.5+x)² = 1/x².
sol: Zero-field point lies on the weaker-charge side, outside.

new.q: Three +3.0 µC charges sit at corners of a right angle: one at the corner, one 0.30 m along x, one 0.30 m along y. What is the net force magnitude on the corner charge in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
new.w: Add the two perpendicular forces as vectors.

new.q: By what factor must you multiply the distance between two charges to make the force twice as large? (decimal)
new.w: F ∝ 1/r², so r ∝ 1/√F.

new.q: By what factor must you multiply the distance to make the force 9 times smaller?
new.w: F ∝ 1/r².

new.q: Two identical hollow metal spheres carry +10 µC and −2 µC. They touch and are separated. Compared with before, the force between them at the same distance:
o: stays attractive and is the same
new.w: After touching each has +4 µC.

new.q: A +Q point charge sits at the center of a thin, neutral metal shell. Just outside the shell, the field is:
o: the same as if Q were alone, pointing outward
new.w: Induced surface charges −Q inside and +Q outside restore the outside field.
sol: Outside, the field looks like Q alone.

new.q: A neutral metal sphere on a stand is near a +Q charge. Which is true?
o: The sphere is attracted even though it has no net charge
new.w: Induction/polarization puts opposite charge nearer.
sol: Nearer −charge pulls harder than the farther +charge pushes.

new.q: A +3q and a −q are fixed apart. A third charge is placed so net force on it is zero. It must be:
o: outside, closer to the smaller (−q) charge
outside, closer to the larger (+3q) charge
new.w: Outside, the weaker charge must be the nearer one to balance it.
sol: Between: both forces point the same way.
Outside near +3q: +3q is both nearer and larger, so it wins.
Outside near −q: nearer balances the smaller size.

new.q: A spark between a charged person and a doorknob is brief and harmless. Which fact best explains why static shocks do not cause lasting current?
o: The charge is tiny, so only a short burst can flow
new.w: Static has high voltage but very little charge.
sol: Thousands of volts can build up.
Only a tiny amount of charge is stored.
The burst ends in a fraction of a second.

new.q: Which situation requires the most care about static sparks?
o: Pumping fuel on a dry day
new.w: Fuel vapor can be ignited by a spark.
sol: Flowing fuel and clothing add charge.
A spark near vapor can start a fire.

new.q: A student measures force at several distances and plots F versus 1/r². The graph is a straight line through the origin. This shows:
o: F does not depend on distance
new.w: A straight line through the origin means direct proportion.

report: Reviewed all 44 hist and 151 static items. Facts/numerics verified in python: no wrong answers found in the shown items (e.g. 1.50 N, 2.70e-4 N, 6.2e12 e, 3.6 N all correct). Fixes: 22 (added accepted text aliases for short-answer items so spelling/phrasing variants are marked right; reworded hist-040/041 whose stems were awkward or imprecise; static-017 re-leveled to core since it is one division; static-083 now says magnitude and a typing format). Deleted 16: hist-011 (dup of hist-019), hist-032..037 (verbatim lookalikes of hist-024..030), hist-043/044 (dup of hist-031/039 and 027), static-051 (history question inside the charge topic, dup of hist), static-035..037 and static-140..142 (lookalike scaling templates; the shown static-045..047 mcq family and static-026..028 already cover them). Remaining doubts: families show only 3 variants, so the full static families 'q1 x# and distance x#' (id 035) and 'cou-scale' (id 140) probably still have more hidden variants that duplicate static-045 family; I could not see their fp keys, so I did not use del_family. Original bank skewed heavily to level 1-2 recall; hist had 36 of 44 level-1 items mostly 'who did X'. New: 144 questions (71 hist, 73 static), about half level 3, including 60 Hz/period, AC line-loss, induction, Maxwell/Hertz, Boolean eval, and superposition, charge sharing, zero-field point, electron acceleration problems. All numerics computed in python (c1_build.py). Static air-breakdown (3e6 V/m) and 1 MΩ wrist strap items are textbook approximations worded as 'about'.
